verdicts.why: Line 86 reads a 32-bit wire length via unsignedExtend and line 87's `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE` is only a cast-safety test, so line 88 allocates up to 2,147,483,646 bytes from untrusted input; nothing else in the file caps it, and readFieldValue cases 'S' (163) and 'x' (211) plus public readLongstr() all reach it.

The overflow grants the peer no capability it lacks: the same seconds field is fully attacker-chosen, so any TTL/ordering/validity value the claim worries about (including 1969 or far-future dates) is already reachable with a plain non-overflowing value such as -1; the evidence is also arithmetically wrong, Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 is ~9.22e15, not ~9.22e18.

The cycle is real and unguarded: readFieldValue case 'F' (181) calls readTable, whose loop at 150 calls readFieldValue, and case 'A' (184) calls readArray, whose loop at 245 calls readFieldValue; no depth parameter is threaded through any of the three signatures and each level costs only ~6 wire bytes ('F' + 4-byte length + 1-byte name length).

Accurate line-for-line: the guard at 87 is a cast-safety test rather than a resource limit, and the allocation at 88 precedes the in.readFully(buffer) at 89, so a ~15-byte crafted table field can force a multi-gigabyte allocation attempt before any byte of the promised payload is shown to exist.

The arithmetic is right (Long.MAX_VALUE*1000 wraps to -1000) but the claimed impact is false: the seconds value is chosen by the same peer, so 'bypass time-based security checks' or a 1969 date needs no overflow at all (send -1), and the overflow only changes which attacker-chosen Date is produced, not who controls it.

Correctly describes lines 86-88: the array size at line 88 comes straight from the wire via unsignedExtend(in.readInt()) at line 86, bounded only by the cast-safety check at 87 (max 2,147,483,646), with no configurable maximum anywhere in the file.

The claim concedes in its own impact field that the overflow 'grants no capability beyond what the attacker already had', which by definition is not a defect; its threshold figure is also wrong by six orders of magnitude (Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 is ~9.2e15 seconds, not ~9.2 billion).

The substance holds: readBytes (83-95) sizes its array from an unsigned 32-bit wire field with only the cast-safety guard at 87; the line citations for readTable/readArray are imprecise (147 and 241 build TruncatedInputStreams, the readBytes reach is via readFieldValue at 150 and 245) but the reachability they assert is real.

The defect is as described at lines 86-88 (unsigned wire length drives new byte[(int)contentLength] with no limit); the parenthetical is off by one (Integer.MAX_VALUE-1 is 2,147,483,646, not 2,147,483,647) but that does not touch the substance.

The primary finding at 86/88 is exactly what the code does; the secondary note is weaker (lines 142 and 240 do read unbounded 32-bit lengths, but a TruncatedInputStream is a wrapper and is not shown to allocate proportionally) yet it does not contradict the main claim.

readFieldValue (158-221) has no depth argument and both recursion edges exist as cited: case 'F' at 181 into readTable's loop at 150, case 'A' at 184 into readArray's loop at 245; readTable's only early exit (line 143, tableLength==0) does not bound nesting.

Line references check out (case 'F' at 180-181, case 'A' at 183-184, loops at 150 and 245) and no depth counter exists in any of the three static methods, so nesting depth is limited only by how many bytes the peer can send.
Every cited line is correct (readTable declared at 139, readArray at 237, recursive calls at 150 and 245, dispatch at 181 and 184) and the mutual recursion is genuinely undepth-limited in this file.

Correct on the mechanism and on the missing depth parameter in the readFieldValue/readTable/readArray signatures (158, 139, 237); its cost estimate is if anything conservative, since each nesting level consumes only about six wire bytes.

Its threshold arithmetic is right, but the impact is not: message-expiration/TTL/audit values the claim lists are already fully settable by the same peer through the ordinary non-overflowing range (about +/-292 million years), so the wrap adds no reachable Date of consequence and no new capability.

Within this file the mechanism is coherent (lines 148 and 244 bound the loops by available(), and neither readTable nor readArray skips the unread remainder of the TruncatedInputStream afterwards, so an early exit really would desynchronise the parent stream), but deciding it requires TruncatedInputStream.available() and the concrete stream the ValueReader constructor (line 57) is handed, neither of which is under the target path.

Same verified mutual recursion (158 -> 181 -> readTable -> 150 -> 158, and 158 -> 184 -> readArray -> 245 -> 158) with no depth counter; the switch default at 216 rejects unknown type bytes but places no limit on legal nested 'F'/'A' values.
Accurate description of readFieldValue (158-221) recursing through readTable (181/150) and readArray (184/245) with no enforced depth limit anywhere in the file.

The core finding at 83-95 is what the code does, though two details are wrong: unsignedExtend explicitly does NOT sign-extend (lines 42-48, `extended & INT_MASK`), and 'multiple 2GB+ arrays' from one message overstates it, since in.readFully at line 89 must succeed before the next field is parsed, so only one oversized array is live before EOFException.
